title: Roadmap 15: Observability, security and testing
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic quizzes that follow the backend interview roadmap: language core, concurrency, DSA habits, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, and LLM/agent engineering.
description: Correlation IDs and tracing, SLOs and error budgets, debugging a slow endpoint, JWT and refresh tokens, authorisation, OWASP and LLM risks, and test strategy.
source: Interview roadmap study plan (Java/Spring Boot and Python/FastAPI)

questions.prompt: A request crosses an API gateway and three services, and one user reports a failure. How do you find every log line for that request?

options.text: Propagate a trace id in headers and add it to the logging context (MDC).
options.why: Right: one id lets you filter logs and traces across services.

options.text: Search each service log around the reported time and compare timestamps.
options.why: Clocks drift and concurrent traffic makes this guesswork.

options.text: Switch every service to debug logging and read the output for that minute.
options.why: Floods storage and still gives no link between services.

options.text: Ask the user to retry the action and watch the network tab of the browser.
options.why: Shows only the client view, not what happened in the services.

questions.explanation: Logs, metrics and traces answer different questions. OpenTelemetry propagates context (W3C traceparent) and the id is added to MDC so every log line carries it.

questions.prompt: A service has a 99.9% availability SLO over a 30 day window. Roughly how much downtime does its error budget allow?

options.text: About 43 minutes.
options.why: Right: 0.1% of 43,200 minutes is about 43 minutes.

options.text: About 4.3 minutes.
options.why: That is the budget for a 99.99% SLO.

options.text: About 7.2 hours.
options.why: That is the budget for a 99% SLO.

options.text: About 1.5 days.
options.why: Far above even 99%; check the percentage arithmetic.

questions.explanation: An SLO is the target, an SLI the measurement. The error budget is 1 minus the SLO; spending it fast should slow releases and page on burn rate, not on every blip.

questions.prompt: The p99 latency of GET /reports jumped from 300 ms to 4 s after last week's release. What is the best first step?

options.text: Open a trace of a slow request and find which span dominates.
options.why: Right: measure before changing anything.

options.text: Add a cache in front of the endpoint immediately, before knowing the cause.
options.why: May hide the cause, and invalidation adds new risk.

options.text: Scale the deployment to twice as many pods and see if latency improves.
options.why: Does not help if the time is spent waiting on one query or call.

options.text: Rewrite the whole handler as asynchronous code and redeploy it.
options.why: A guess; blocking is not shown to be the problem.

questions.explanation: Then check the diff and metrics, use EXPLAIN on the slow query, look for N+1 queries, and re-measure after each change.

questions.prompt: Why use refresh-token rotation, where each refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one?

options.text: A reused old token reveals theft, so the server can revoke the token family.
options.why: Right: the thief or the user will present an already used token.

options.text: It lets access tokens live for a whole year without any extra risk.
options.why: Rotation protects refresh tokens; long access tokens stay hard to revoke.

options.text: It removes the need for the server to store any refresh-token state at all.
options.why: Detecting reuse needs server-side state.

options.text: It encrypts the JWT payload so clients cannot read the claims.
options.why: Rotation is about token lifecycle, not payload confidentiality.

questions.explanation: Keep access tokens short-lived and refresh tokens revocable and stored server-side. Sessions with server state revoke easily; stateless JWTs need short expiry or a denylist.

questions.prompt: True or false: authorisation must be enforced on the server for each request, for example with @PreAuthorize, because hiding a button in the UI does not stop a direct API call.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: clients are untrusted and anyone can call the API directly.

options.text: False
options.why: The UI is not a security boundary.

questions.explanation: AuthN says who you are, AuthZ says what you may do. Also check object-level ownership (the order belongs to this user), not only the role.

questions.prompt: True or false: the payload of a standard signed JWT is encrypted, so it is safe to put secrets such as passwords in its claims.

options.text: True
options.why: Signing does not hide the contents.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the payload is only base64url-encoded; the signature prevents tampering, not reading.

questions.explanation: Keep claims minimal and non-sensitive. Verify signature, expiry, issuer and audience on every request.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. Which defences are appropriate?

options.text: Use parameterised queries to prevent SQL injection.
options.why: Right: data is never parsed as SQL.

options.text: Use anti-CSRF tokens or SameSite cookies for state-changing requests authenticated by cookies.
options.why: Right: stops other sites triggering actions with the browser cookie.

options.text: Treat retrieved documents and model output as untrusted, give the agent least-privilege tools, and filter by tenant.
options.why: Right: limits prompt injection and cross-tenant leaks.

options.text: Escape quote characters with a regular expression as the main SQL injection defence.
options.why: Escaping is fragile; use parameters.

options.text: Commit API keys to a private repository because only the team can see it.
options.why: Secrets belong in a secret manager; repository history leaks.

questions.explanation: A prompt-injected agent that can read every tenant's data will leak it, so authorisation must be enforced in the tools and queries, not in the prompt.

questions.prompt: A repository class uses Postgres-specific SQL (a JSONB filter and ON CONFLICT). How do you best test it?

options.text: An integration test against real Postgres via Testcontainers.
options.why: Right: exercises the real SQL, dialect and migrations.

options.text: A unit test that mocks the repository interface and verifies the call was made.
options.why: Never runs the SQL, so the query bugs stay hidden.

options.text: A test against H2 in-memory, assuming it behaves just like Postgres.
options.why: Dialect differences can pass here and fail in production.

options.text: Skip automated tests and check the query by hand once.
options.why: Not repeatable and regressions go unnoticed.

questions.explanation: Mock external boundaries in fast unit tests, use real dependencies for integration tests, and use contract tests to keep service consumers and providers in agreement.
